The *Jaṭila Sutta* (Ud 1.9; PTS Ud 6) is the ninth discourse in the opening chapter (Bodhivagga) of the *Udāna* [SuttaCentral]. According to the summary recorded by SuttaCentral, the sutta conveys the teaching that the mind is cleansed and purified not through external ritual bathing or ablutions, but through truth and rectitude [SuttaCentral]. SuttaCentral lists 16 translations of the text in 13 languages, including an English translation by Bhikkhu Sujato [SuttaCentral]. None of the secondary literature passages in the dossier directly address this sutta; references titled *Jaṭila Sutta* in the dossier refer instead to the homonymous discourse featuring King Pasenadi and spies disguised as matted-hair ascetics found elsewhere in the canon (SN 3.11 / Ud 6.2).

The verse material of the discourse is widely shared across early Buddhist poetic literature. SuttaCentral identifies passage-level parallels in Sanskrit and Chinese recensions of the *Udānavarga* tradition: the Sanskrit *Udānavarga* (UV 33 / UVS 33, *Brāhmaṇavarga*), the Chinese *Chuyao jing* (T 212.34), and the *Faji yousong jing* (T 213.33) [SuttaCentral]. Resembling verse parallels also occur extensively in the "Brahmin" chapters of canonical verse collections, notably the Pali *Dhammapada* (Dhp 393), the Chinese *Dharmapada* (T 210.35), the Gāndhārī *Dharmapada* (G-Dhp 1–50), the Patna *Dharmapada* (P-Dhp 34–49), and the Tibetan *Udānavarga* (Uv Kg 33) [SuttaCentral]. The text is also cited in the paracanonical *Nettippakaraṇa* (Ne 37) [SuttaCentral]. Furthermore, DharmaNexus identifies 25 Pali-internal reuse matches across five texts, sharing formulaic prose narrative segments with the *Māra Saṁyutta* (SN 4), the Vinaya *Mahākhandhaka* (Kd 1), the *Aṭṭhakanipāta* (AN 8), the *Chakkanipāta* (AN 6), and the *Apadāna-aṭṭhakathā* [DharmaNexus].
